newsitem.title: UK: Britain's "Road To Hell" celebrates 10th birthday.
newsitem.headline: Britain's "Road To Hell" celebrates 10th birthday.

text.p: The M25, the orbital motorway around London often called the world's largest carpark because of chronic traffic jams, is 10 years old on Tuesday.

Immortalised in the pop song "Road to Hell", the M25 is the longest city bypass in the world and Europe's busiest road. Every London motorist has an M25 story that could be headlined, "I sat for two hours and we hardly moved an inch."
From the day the motorway was opened in 1986 by then Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, the one billion pound ($1.6 billion) ring road has been criticised.
The environmental group Friends of the Earth calls the M25 a "complete failure," because it encouraged people to abandon public transport in favour of the motor car.
"It is the ultimate transport disaster," said FOE spokesman Simon Festing. "It has generated so much extra traffic. The M25 was heavily congested soon after it was opened."
The M25 is 117 miles (185 km) long and its used by around 700,000 cars during London's morning rush hour.

Congestion inspired British singer Chris Rea to write the hit song "Road to Hell" in 1989. In it Rea laments the traffic jams, which Britain's biggest car-breakdown service, the Automobile Association, says total 73 miles on any given Monday.
Britain's Department of Transport disbelieves the ditty.
"The song is extremely unfair," said Mark Howard, spokesman for the Department of Transport's Highways Agency.
"The M25 is an undoubted success and works extremely well most of the time. There are occasional hiccups especially when there are accidents," he said.
"The answer in a lot of ways to the congestion is in the hands of the motorist. They need to drive more carefully."
The idea for a orbital highway skirting London dates back to 1905 but the go-ahead for the project was not given until 1975.
Civil engineers who worked on the original design said the then government underestimated the amount of traffic.
"Our firm told (government) officials that their estimates were far too low and that the M25 would be crammed from day one," said a civil engineer who advised the government.
The engineer, who wished to remain anonymous, said the politicians of the day "decided to go for the cheapest option" by building a road that was only three lanes wide.

"The simple fact is they just did not want to spend the money to allow for a leap in demand. It would have cost more initially but now they are having to spend more money on maintenance and are widening the motorway which is expensive."
By the end of the decade, around a quarter of the M25 will have been widened to four lanes.
The AA believes that overall the M25 is a benefit to the country's 25.4 million motorists as it enables people to bypass London when going from the south of England to the north.
Love it or hate it, the M25 has rarely been out of the headlines and it holds a morbid fascination for many drivers.
William Allen, 84, spent two days circling the motorway after getting lost on the way to his daughter's house.
A police car once had to rescue an elderly woman who somehow ended up cycling the wrong way down an outside lane.
She was seen holding her hat with one hand against the slip streams from dodging vehicles while steering with the other.
